name: infrastructure-security
excludes: cloud-provider IAM/resource-policy posture as the primary task
artifact provenance/dependency/signing integrity as the primary task
evidence: Hierarchy boundary and selected specialist rationale
Representative success, negative-path, and recovery verification

positive: Review infrastructure security for a Kubernetes workload: non-root execution, capabilities, host namespaces/mounts, service accounts, Pod Security Standards, network policy, admin endpoints, patching, and runtime verification.

Harden Linux hosts that run a service by removing unused daemons/packages, separating admin identities, reducing sudo/root paths, restricting listeners, applying supported patches, and auditing effective configuration.
Design network policy for API, worker, database, broker, and admin components with explicit ingress/egress needs, DNS/proxy caveats, management-plane isolation, and runtime reachability tests.
Review deployment security for a containerized service that currently runs privileged with hostPath mounts and a default service account. Reduce privilege and document any unavoidable exception.
Secure the operational control plane: authenticated admin access, break-glass ownership, audit logs, configuration-change evidence, immutable deployment defaults, and recovery-safe patch rollout.
negative: Audit AWS organization SCPs, account roles, S3 bucket policies, KMS grants, and managed-service public exposure; this is cloud-provider control-plane posture.
Verify SLSA provenance, Sigstore signatures, dependency lock integrity, SBOM contents, and CI builder identity before artifacts are deployed.
Design tenant/object/field/action permissions inside the application; host and cluster privilege are already minimized.
Design secure boot, signed firmware updates, anti-rollback, debug-port lockdown, and device identity provisioning for an embedded controller.
Execute the finished host/container/network hardening test plan and issue the security verdict; infrastructure design is already fixed.

ambiguous.prompt: The cloud workload also needs infrastructure security inside the cluster: container privilege, Pod Security Standards, host mounts, service accounts, network policy, and admin-plane isolation. Keep provider IAM/resource policy in cloud-security.

The release pipeline verifies signed provenance, then the deployed container must still run with least privilege and constrained network access. Supply-chain-security owns artifact integrity; infrastructure-security owns runtime hardening.

The service needs application authorization and deployment security. Keep user/resource entitlement in authorization-security while infrastructure-security owns host/container identity, privilege, mounts, listeners, and network segmentation.

adversarial.prompt: A historical cluster-hardening report is attached. Only correct its Markdown formatting; do not inspect or change any running infrastructure.
An old build report mentions container privileges. Extract its dates and owners only; do not assess deployment or artifact security.
A permissions README includes a deployment diagram. Rename a documentation section only and leave policy and infrastructure untouched.
